Wilderness Tests
WIL-der-ness tests
noun phrase (testing in the wilderness)
From the recurring biblical theme of the wilderness as the place of God's proving of His people; Israel's forty years and Christ's forty days the chief instances.

📖 Biblical Definition

The wilderness tests are the trials by which God proves His people in the desert, the place He appoints for humbling, sifting, and the manifesting of what is in the heart. Of Israel's forty years Moses said, “Thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no.” The wilderness was no accident of geography but a school of faith, where God fed them with manna, gave water from the rock, and tested whether they would trust and obey. Israel largely failed—murmuring, lusting, tempting God, and falling in the day of provocation—and these things, the apostle says, were written for our admonition, that we sin not as they sinned. Where the first Israel failed, the true Israel triumphed: the Lord Jesus was led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil, and where Adam fell in a garden of plenty and Israel fell in the desert of want, Christ overcame, answering every temptation with the written Word, “It is written.” The dictionary marks the wilderness tests as a pattern of the Christian life: God leads His people through seasons of want and trial, not to destroy but to humble and prove them, that they may learn to live by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God. The proper response is not the murmuring of unbelief but the trust that knows the same God who led into the wilderness will lead through it, having Himself, in Christ, passed the test His people failed.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The trials by which God proves His people in the desert (Deuteronomy 8:2); Israel's forty years and Christ's forty days the chief instances—where the first Israel murmured and fell, the true Israel overcame by the written Word.

expand to see more

WILDERNESS TESTS, noun phrase. The trials by which God proves His people in the desert, to humble and to manifest the heart.

Israel's forty years were to humble and prove them, to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2).

They largely failed—murmuring, lusting, and provoking God in the day of temptation.

These things were written for our admonition (1 Corinthians 10:11).

Christ, the true Israel, overcame in the wilderness by the written Word (Matthew 4:1).

📖 Key Scripture

De 8:2 — "And thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no."

Mt 4:1 — "Then was Jesus led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil."

Heb 3:8 — "Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness:"

1 Co 10:11 — "Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the prosperity gospel that denies God leads His people through seasons of want, and the murmuring heart that reads trial as God's rejection.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints seasons of trial to humble and prove His people. The prosperity gospel teaches that the favour of God means continual plenty and ease, so that the wilderness—want, hunger, hardship—must be a sign of insufficient faith or hidden sin. But God Himself led Israel into the wilderness to humble and to prove them, and led His own Son there to be tempted. The desert is not the mark of God's absence but often the school of His nearest dealing.

The opposite corruption is the murmuring of unbelief, which reads every trial as God's rejection and turns, like Israel, to complaint and the longing for Egypt. The apostle warns that these things were written for our admonition. The dictionary recovers the wilderness tests as a pattern of sanctification: God leads His people through want to teach them to live by every word of His mouth, and the believer's part is not to murmur but to trust—remembering that the Lord Jesus, the true Israel, passed in the desert the very test His people failed, and now leads them through their own wilderness as a faithful Captain who knows the way.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew midbar (wilderness, desert) and nasah (to test, prove); the forty years and forty days mark the wilderness as God's appointed place of proving.

expand to see more

Midbar, Hebrew, wilderness or desert, the place of God's proving of Israel.

Nasah, Hebrew, to test, try, or prove, as God proved Israel's heart.

Massah and Meribah, the “temptation” and “strife” where Israel provoked God.

The forty years of Israel answer the forty days of Christ's temptation.

“It is written” (Greek gegraptai) is the Lord's threefold answer to the tempter.

Usage

"The pastor preached the wilderness tests to comfort the suffering, for God leads His own through want to prove them."

"He warned against the murmuring of Israel, written for our admonition that we trust and not complain."

"She saw that Christ overcame in the desert where Israel fell, and followed her Captain through the trial."
